title: 'Can't Indian Coaches Develop Indian Hockey?': PR Sreejesh's Ouster Exposes a Systemic Blind Spot
excerpt: Two-time Olympic medallist delivered five podium finishes as junior coach — then lost his job to a preference for foreign expertise
body:
Parattu Raveendran Sreejesh has never been one to go quietly. The man who spent two decades between the posts for India — the man who carried his team to consecutive Olympic bronze medals in Tokyo and Paris — has now found himself on the outside of the very system he tried to rebuild from within.

## The Coaching Record That Wasn't Enough

When Sreejesh retired from international hockey after the 2024 Paris Olympics, where he saved India's bronze medal with a legendary final-quarter performance, Hockey India appointed him as head coach of the junior men's (U-21) team. It seemed like a natural fit: India's most decorated modern goalkeeper, transitioning from player to mentor, tasked with nurturing the next generation.

The results spoke for themselves. In roughly 17 months at the helm, Sreejesh's junior team delivered five tournament podium finishes, including a bronze medal at the 2025 FIH Junior World Cup — India's best result at the tournament in years — and another bronze at the Sultan of Johor Cup. By any reasonable measure, the programme was thriving.

Then, earlier this month, Sreejesh revealed that Hockey India had effectively ended his tenure. His contract was not renewed. The reason, he alleged, was painfully simple: the senior men's team chief coach preferred a foreign head coach for the junior programme.

## 'Can't Indian Coaches Develop Indian Hockey?'

"Can't Indian coaches develop Indian hockey?" Sreejesh asked in a pointed public statement that ricocheted across Indian sports media. It was not a tantrum — it was a question that has lingered over Indian sport for decades, now given voice by someone whose credentials are beyond dispute.

Sreejesh specifically pointed to the contradiction between official rhetoric and practice. In March, Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya had publicly backed Sreejesh, endorsing his vision for junior development ahead of the LA 2028 Olympics. Yet within weeks, the federation moved in a different direction entirely.

Hockey India President Dr Dilip Tirkey pushed back, denying that Sreejesh was fired. The federation stated that his contract had simply ended in December 2025 and that he was offered a "developmental role" — a vague reassignment that Sreejesh declined, viewing it as a demotion dressed in diplomatic language.

## The Systemic Question

The Sreejesh episode is not an isolated grievance. It sits within a broader pattern across Indian sport, where federations frequently turn to foreign coaches even when domestic alternatives exist. The Indian hockey programme has cycled through foreign coaches for decades — from Roelant Oltmans to Graham Reid to Craig Fulton — with varying results. The assumption, often unexamined, is that foreign expertise is inherently superior.

Sreejesh's argument is not that foreign coaches have no place. It is that Indian coaches are rarely given the opportunity to prove themselves at the highest levels, and that when they do produce results — as he demonstrably did — the goalposts shift.

## The Diaspora Perspective

For Indian hockey fans abroad — and there are millions of them, from the UK to Canada to Australia and the Gulf — this controversy strikes a nerve that extends well beyond sport. Many NRIs who grew up watching hockey as India's national game have seen it decline, revive, and now grapple with questions of institutional identity.

The larger issue mirrors a familiar debate in the diaspora: can India's institutions trust homegrown talent, or will they perpetually defer to external validation? NRI hockey communities, which have organised viewing parties for Olympic matches from Toronto to Dubai, find themselves asking whether the system that produced Sreejesh can also trust Sreejesh.

The irony is hard to miss. India's greatest modern hockey goalkeeper — the man who literally saved the nation's Olympic dream twice — has been told that his coaching tenure, however successful, is not quite what the system is looking for.

## What Comes Next

Hockey India has not yet named Sreejesh's replacement as junior coach. The controversy has drawn attention from lawmakers and sports administrators, with several former players publicly backing Sreejesh's stance. Whether the federation reverses course remains to be seen, but the conversation Sreejesh has started — about the value India places on its own sporting expertise — is unlikely to fade.

The LA 2028 Olympics are barely two years away. India's junior pipeline feeds directly into the senior squad. Whatever Hockey India decides, the clock is ticking, and the architect who was building that pipeline has just been shown the door.
